description: Thorium is a weakly radioactive light silver metal with atomic number 90 that tarnishes olive grey when exposed to air. It is moderately soft, malleable, and has a high melting point of 1750 °C. As an electropositive actinide, its chemistry is dominated by the +4 oxidation state and it is quite reactive, capable of igniting in air when finely divided.
uses: Thorium is used as an alloying element in TIG welding electrodes and in strengthening magnesium. It has been used in high-end optics, scientific instrumentation, broadcast vacuum tubes, and as the light source in gas mantles, though these uses have become marginal. It is also used in coating tungsten wire, controlling grain size in electric lamps, high-temperature crucibles, glasses for lenses, heat-resistant ceramics, aircraft engines, and light bulbs, and ocean science uses thorium isotope ratios to understand ancient oceans.
characteristics: Thorium is a moderately soft, paramagnetic, bright silvery metal that is very ductile and can be cold-rolled, swaged, and drawn. At room temperature it has a face-centred cubic crystal structure with a bulk modulus of 54 GPa and becomes superconductive below 1.4 K. It has a density of approximately 11.5 to 11.66 g/cm³ and is nearly half as dense as uranium and plutonium while being harder than both.
